summary: DHCPv6 gives IPv6 hosts addresses and configuration, but its messages can carry identifiers that let others track a device. This informational RFC analyzes the privacy issues of DHCPv6 use by Internet users. It is an analysis of the present situation and proposes no solutions.

plainLanguage.summary: DHCPv6 helps an IPv6 device obtain network configuration, but its messages may reveal information about that device. This RFC describes what can be learned from those messages and how the information can be used to track or identify a client.

subtitle: Privacy risks from identifiers and other information carried in DHCPv6 messages.

tldr.problem: DHCPv6 messages can disclose stable identifiers, device details, or clues about where a client has connected.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC inventories identifying fields and options, reviews existing address and DNS mechanisms, and describes attacks that use the information.
tldr.outcome: It analyzes privacy risks in DHCPv6 but proposes no protocol changes; it points to RFC 7844 as an example of later work.

sections.title: Scope and Stable Identifiers
sections.content:
DHCPv6 provides addressing and configuration information to IPv6 hosts. Its messages can contain identifiers and other details that reveal a device type, operating system, or networks the device has visited. This RFC analyzes privacy risks for clients that connect to different networks.

A stable identifier is information disclosed by a client that does not change, or changes infrequently, and is unique for that client in a context. Examples in the RFC include a MAC address, client identifier, or hostname. The document analyzes the situation and does not propose protocol changes.
sections.plainLanguage: Some DHCPv6 information can stay the same when a device moves between networks. Observers may use those stable details to recognize or learn about the device.

sections.title: Information in DHCPv6 Messages
sections.content:
The RFC discusses several sources of identifying information. A DHCP Unique Identifier (DUID) is intended to remain stable, and the default DUID-LLT form is based on a link-layer address. Other options can carry a hostname, vendor information, requested configuration options, or a client's previous address.

Relay agents may add subscriber, interface, remote, or link-layer information. These relay options usually travel between the relay and the server within the operator's network, so the RFC distinguishes them from information available to someone observing the client's last wireless hop.
sections.plainLanguage: DHCPv6 options can reveal a device identifier, hostname, vendor, or earlier address. Relay agents may add other details that are normally carried inside the network operator's infrastructure.

sections.title: Temporary Addresses, DNS, and Allocation
sections.content:
The RFC notes that temporary addresses may be renewed by some clients, which can reduce their privacy benefit. Publishing a client's IPv6 address in publicly available DNS can expose its address and hostname. A stable hostname can link a client across network attachments even when its address changes.

Address allocation also affects privacy. Sequential allocation makes addresses more predictable, and identifier-based allocation can expose an identifier in the address. Random allocation reduces some forms of correlation, but other DHCPv6 fields may still disclose identifying information.
sections.plainLanguage: Temporary or random addresses do not hide every clue. A hostname or client identifier can still link a device to earlier connections.

sections.title: Attacks and the Limits of the Analysis
sections.content:
The RFC describes attacks that use DHCPv6 information to fingerprint devices and operating systems, infer location, identify previously visited networks, or correlate activity over time. It also discusses pervasive monitoring, finding addresses or hostnames through DNS, and misuse of lease-query mechanisms to obtain location information.

The document does not prescribe a fix. It notes that, in current practice as described by the RFC, client authentication can reveal additional client information and may conflict with client privacy. RFC 7844 is cited as an example of later work proposing protocol changes.
sections.plainLanguage: Observers may combine DHCPv6 details to infer a device's type, location, or past connections. This RFC describes those risks but leaves protocol changes to other work.
